newsitem.title: USA: Brave new world on Wall Street; investors unfazed by Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: Brave new world on Wall Street; investors unfazed by Greenspan.

text.p: It's a brave new world on Wall Street and investors are not being scared off by talk that the stock market could be headed for a fall, despite gloom-and-doom warnings from the Federal Reserve chief.

Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan, whose every utterance is put under a magnifying glass for clues to the central bank's interest rate policy, has rattled investors over the last few months with hints that stocks are overvalued.

Greenspan reemerged on Wednesday but this time, the emperor of interest rates changed his tune, and said stocks might not be over-priced after all, easing investors' fears that the central bank would tighten monetary policy to lasso the bull market.
The Fed chief said he did not believe in using monetary policy as a tool to influence stock prices.
And, Greenspan even went so far as to say that the market might be reasonably priced, provided that analysts' forecasts of future corporate earnings are correct.

"It's pretty obvious that if you look at a normal pricing model for stocks, what you get is a not unreasonable level of prices if the earnings forecasts which the analysts are publishing are accurate," said Greenspan.

Investors applauded the comments and boosted the Dow Jones industrial average, lifting the index of 30 blue-chip stocks. In late trading Friday, the index was up 56.57 points at 7,001.27, putting it within flirting distance of its record high close of 7,067.46 set on Feb. 18. For the week, it gained 123.53 points.
The Fed chief, who believes that investors have impossibly optimistic views of stocks, is apparently worried that a market collapse could be the source of economic instability.

He has been trying to convince investors to control their appetite for stocks. But Greenspan he has had limited success since he first sounded a warning in December with his famous irrational exuberance talk that caused a one-day selloff followed by a 10 percent rally.

In late February, he suggested that stock prices might be too high, touching off a series of rapid-fire sell-offs that wiped out more than 160 points from the Dow Jones as nervous investors feared that Greenspan would raise interest rates to reinforce his warnings.
But the market has since recovered all of its loss, buoyed by pent-up demand.
Wall Streeters have stuck to the view that 'We'll believe the end of the bull market when we see it.'
Investors had another reason this week to toast the Fed chief, who now appears to have joined the camp of people who believe that this is a golden age for stocks.
The experts have been saying all along that the market reflects a new economic climate -- one that will bring faster growth with shorter recessions and lower inflation.

"We are looking at the longest running winning streak for stocks in modern times and this is due to a change in the economy," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist for Fahnestock & Co. "The economic cycles seem to be more manageable and the stretches of good economic numbers have held up longer."
He said the average investor has already caught on to this new era, propelling the stock market to dizzying heights amid the longest period of consecutive double-digit earnings increases in 50 years.
"The small investor seems to be geared to staying the course and there is a sense that patience pays off and they've not reacted to downdrafts in the market," Ackerman said.
Indeed, the market's run-up has been unprecedented.

The Standard & Poor's index of 500 companies has had an annual total return over the last 20 years of more than 14.5 percent vs. a gain of only 8.4 percent for U.S. stocks over the last 207 years, says Barton Biggs, global investment strategist for Morgan Stanley.
Are there more succulent opportunities for hungry stock investors?

"The issue of whether the mean (rate of return) is now higher is an incredibly important one, because if the answer is yes, equities as the truly superior asset class should be a much higher percentage of portfolios, since there is no evidence that the real returns on other assets like bonds and real estate have changed," Biggs said.

The experts say the action of the Fed was the one constant threat to the stock market, and they expect that there will be a healthy smattering of fear, when the central bank's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee meets on March 25 to weigh monetary policy.

"The action of the market over the last few sessions may have reflected the concern at a coming quarter-of-a-percentage-point rate rise, but the investors now seem to be comfortable with the prospect if the Fed does raise interest rates, it would be manageable," Ackerman said."
"But again, if the Fed does not raise rates, the market could move higher," he said.
The stock market does not like higher interest rates because they tend to slow consumer spending and eat into corporate earnings.
Some Fed watchers believe that Greenspan will indeed pull the interest rate trigger this month.

"Mr. Greenspan seems to be setting the stage for a 25-basis-point hike in the federal funds rate at the March 25 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee," says Edward Yardeni, chief economist for Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

"I don't expect more than that because I believe that inflation will remain too low to justify a series of rate hikes as in 1994," he said. "I also believe that such a rate hike would be mostly symbolic."
The central bank went on a rate boosting spree in 1994, after Greenspan warned early in that year that rising economic growth might force the Fed to launch a pre-emptive strike on inflation.

The Fed struck furiously -- boosting the Fed fund rate on Feb. 4, 1994, and went on to tighten six more times, raising the key interest rate from 3 percent to 6 percent by February 1995. The fund rate has since been lowered and currently hovers at 5.25 percent, but it is still well above its early 1994 level.
